free-chlorine.name: Free Chlorine
free-chlorine.shortDescription: The active, unsaturated chlorine available to sanitize pool water.
free-chlorine.longDescription: Free chlorine (FC) is the portion of chlorine in pool water that has not yet reacted with contaminants. It exists primarily as hypochlorous acid (HOCl) and hypochlorite ion (OCl−). HOCl is the active sanitizing form and is 40–80× more effective than OCl−. The ratio of HOCl to OCl− is determined by pH — lower pH means more HOCl. Free chlorine must be maintained above the minimum level dictated by the cyanuric acid concentration.

combined-chlorine.name: Combined Chlorine
combined-chlorine.shortDescription: Chlorine that has reacted with contaminants and is no longer effective for sanitization.
combined-chlorine.longDescription: Combined chlorine (CC) is the difference between total chlorine and free chlorine. It consists primarily of chloramines — compounds formed when chlorine reacts with ammonia, urea, and other nitrogen compounds from bathers. Chloramines are responsible for the "pool smell," eye irritation, and respiratory irritation often mistakenly blamed on too much chlorine. When CC exceeds 0.5 ppm, breakpoint chlorination (shock treatment) is required.

total-chlorine.name: Total Chlorine
total-chlorine.shortDescription: The sum of free chlorine and combined chlorine in pool water.
total-chlorine.longDescription: Total chlorine (TC) equals free chlorine plus combined chlorine. Most DPD-based test kits measure total chlorine directly, while free chlorine requires a separate reagent. Combined chlorine is calculated as TC minus FC. Total chlorine by itself tells you little about water safety — what matters is the free chlorine level and how much has become combined.
total-chlorine.idealRange: Same as FC target (CC should be 0)

bromine.name: Bromine
bromine.shortDescription: A halogen sanitizer commonly used in hot tubs that remains effective at higher pH and temperatures.
bromine.longDescription: Bromine is an alternative to chlorine as a pool and spa sanitizer. It is more stable than chlorine at high temperatures and high pH, making it popular for hot tubs. Unlike chlorine, bromine can be regenerated by adding an oxidizer — the bromamines formed are still effective sanitizers. Bromine cannot be stabilized with cyanuric acid, making it unsuitable for outdoor pools exposed to direct sunlight. It is sold as BCDMH tablets or as a two-part sodium bromide / oxidizer system.

cyanuric-acid.name: Cyanuric Acid
cyanuric-acid.shortDescription: A chemical stabilizer that protects chlorine from UV degradation in outdoor pools.
cyanuric-acid.longDescription: Cyanuric acid (CYA) — also called stabilizer or conditioner — binds to free chlorine to protect it from UV photolysis. Without CYA, outdoor pool chlorine can degrade to near-zero within 30–60 minutes in direct sunlight. However, CYA also reduces chlorine's activity. As CYA increases, the minimum effective free chlorine level must increase proportionally. CYA above 80–100 ppm causes chlorine lock, where chlorine is present but largely ineffective. CYA cannot be reduced chemically — only dilution by partial drain and refill removes it.

calcium-hardness.name: Calcium Hardness
calcium-hardness.shortDescription: The concentration of dissolved calcium in pool water, affecting scaling and corrosion tendency.
calcium-hardness.longDescription: Calcium hardness (CH) is the measure of dissolved calcium ions in pool water. It is one of the five variables in the Langelier Saturation Index. Water with low calcium is aggressive — it will dissolve calcium from plaster, grout, and equipment. Water with high calcium is scale-forming — calcium carbonate precipitates on surfaces and inside equipment. The ideal range depends on pool surface type: plaster pools need higher calcium (200–400 ppm) than vinyl or fiberglass pools (150–250 ppm). Calcium hardness can only be lowered through partial drain and refill.

salt.name: Salt
salt.shortDescription: Sodium chloride dissolved in pool water to enable chlorine generation by a salt chlorinator.
salt.longDescription: Pool salt is pure sodium chloride (NaCl) added to pool water for use with a salt chlorinator (also called a saltwater generator or SWCG). The system electrolytically converts dissolved salt into hypochlorous acid — the same active disinfectant as manually added chlorine. Salt level must stay within the system's specified range (typically 2,700–3,400 ppm) for the cell to operate efficiently. Salt does not evaporate; the level only drops through dilution from rain or water replacement. Human sweat is saltier than a properly maintained salt pool.

total-dissolved-solids.name: Total Dissolved Solids
total-dissolved-solids.shortDescription: The cumulative concentration of all dissolved matter in pool water.
total-dissolved-solids.longDescription: Total dissolved solids (TDS) is the sum of all inorganic and organic substances dissolved in pool water — minerals, chemicals, byproducts of sanitization, bather waste, and more. TDS increases over time as chemicals are added and water evaporates. High TDS can reduce chemical effectiveness, cause foaming in hot tubs, and contribute to cloudy water. The only remedy is partial or full water replacement. In hot tubs, TDS above 1,500 ppm over the baseline is a standard trigger for water change.
total-dissolved-solids.idealRange: Below 2,000 ppm (pools); below 1,500 ppm above baseline (spas)

phosphate.name: Phosphate
phosphate.shortDescription: A nutrient compound in pool water that can fuel algae growth.
phosphate.longDescription: Phosphates are compounds containing phosphorus (PO4³⁻) that enter pool water from bather waste, lawn fertilizer runoff, fill water, and certain pool chemicals. Phosphates are a primary nutrient for algae. While low phosphate levels alone do not cause algae (chlorine control is paramount), very high phosphate levels (above 500–1,000 ppb) can reduce chlorine effectiveness and increase algae risk. Phosphate removers are available but their necessity is debated — good chlorine management prevents algae regardless of phosphate level.

copper.name: Copper
copper.shortDescription: A metal that can enter pool water from ionizers, algaecides, or corroded equipment, causing green staining.
copper.longDescription: Copper can enter pool water from copper-based algaecides, copper-silver ionizers, copper pipes, or from the fill water itself. At elevated levels (above 0.3 ppm), copper causes green staining of pool surfaces and hair. This is often confused with algae but is actually copper oxidation. Copper staining is treated with sequestrants and by identifying and eliminating the copper source. Corrosive water (low LSI) accelerates copper leaching from equipment.

iron.name: Iron
iron.shortDescription: A metal dissolved in pool water that causes rust-brown staining when oxidized.
iron.longDescription: Iron in pool water typically comes from well water used to fill the pool or from corroded steel equipment. When chlorine is added, dissolved ferrous iron (Fe²⁺) is oxidized to ferric iron (Fe³⁺), which is insoluble and precipitates as rust-brown staining on pool walls, floors, and equipment. Treatment involves metal sequestrants to keep iron in solution, then gradual removal through filtration. Prevention focuses on fill water quality and maintaining a slightly positive LSI to prevent equipment corrosion.

manganese.name: Manganese
manganese.shortDescription: A dissolved metal that causes black or purple staining in pool water.
manganese.longDescription: Manganese enters pool water through well water or certain fill water sources. Like iron, it stains pool surfaces when oxidized — manganese stains are typically black or dark brown/purple rather than the rust-red of iron. Metal sequestrants hold manganese in solution to prevent precipitation. Testing with a metal test kit distinguishes manganese from other staining causes. Thorough filtration after sequestrant treatment gradually removes manganese from the water.

hydrogen-peroxide.name: Hydrogen Peroxide
hydrogen-peroxide.shortDescription: An oxidizer used in non-chlorine pool systems and as an emergency chlorine neutralizer.
hydrogen-peroxide.longDescription: Hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) is used as an oxidizer in biguanide (polyhexamethylene biguanide, or PHMB) pool systems, which use hydrogen peroxide rather than chlorine for sanitization. In chlorine pools, hydrogen peroxide can be used to rapidly reduce excess chlorine in emergencies, but the two chemicals react violently if mixed in concentrated form — always add to pool water separately, never mix directly. Hydrogen peroxide-based systems require dedicated equipment and are incompatible with chlorine.

ozone.name: Ozone
ozone.shortDescription: A powerful oxidizer generated on-site and injected into pool water as a supplemental sanitizer.
ozone.longDescription: Ozone (O₃) is a powerful oxidizing agent generated on-site by UV lamps or corona discharge generators and injected into pool return water. It rapidly destroys organic compounds, chloramines, and pathogens. Because ozone dissipates quickly (it does not accumulate in pool water), it must always be used alongside a residual sanitizer — typically free chlorine at reduced levels. Ozone does not replace chlorine; it reduces the chlorine demand and helps maintain water clarity and quality with less total chemical use.

biguanide.name: Biguanide
biguanide.shortDescription: A chlorine-free sanitizer system using polyhexamethylene biguanide (PHMB) as the primary disinfectant.
biguanide.longDescription: Biguanide (sold as Baquacil, SoftSwim, and similar brands) is a chlorine-free pool sanitization system using polyhexamethylene biguanide (PHMB) as the sanitizer and hydrogen peroxide as the oxidizer. It does not interact with CYA, pH resistance is broader, and it does not bleach surfaces or swimwear. However, biguanide is incompatible with chlorine — switching between systems requires a complete water change. It is more expensive than chlorine and some users experience algae resistance issues. Not recommended for hot tubs.

ph.name: pH
ph.shortDescription: The measure of hydrogen ion concentration indicating acidity or alkalinity of pool water.
ph.longDescription: pH is the scale from 0 to 14 measuring how acidic or alkaline pool water is. A pH of 7.0 is neutral; below 7.0 is acidic; above 7.0 is alkaline. Pool water should be maintained between 7.2 and 7.6. Below 7.2, water is corrosive — it irritates eyes and skin and attacks surfaces and equipment. Above 7.8, chlorine effectiveness drops dramatically (at pH 8.0 only 22% of chlorine is active vs. 67% at pH 7.2) and scale forms. pH is affected by every chemical addition and by CO₂ off-gassing.

orp.name: ORP
orp.shortDescription: Oxidation-Reduction Potential — an electrical measurement of water's sanitizing capacity.
orp.longDescription: Oxidation-Reduction Potential (ORP) measures the water's ability to oxidize or sanitize — expressed in millivolts (mV). A higher ORP indicates greater sanitizing capacity. Unlike ppm-based chlorine testing, ORP directly measures chlorine's effectiveness considering both concentration and pH. The World Health Organization and many public health authorities specify a minimum ORP of 650 mV for swimming pools. ORP sensors are used in automated chemical control systems to maintain consistent sanitizing capacity regardless of bather load variations.

temperature.name: Temperature
temperature.shortDescription: Water temperature in °F or °C, affecting chemical reactions, chlorine demand, and comfort.
temperature.longDescription: Water temperature directly affects pool and spa water chemistry. Higher temperatures accelerate chlorine demand (halving with every 10°C/18°F drop), shift pH upward, increase scaling tendency (higher LSI), and increase CO₂ off-gassing. For hot tubs, temperature is also a primary safety parameter — temperatures above 104°F can cause hyperthermia. For the LSI calculation, water temperature is a required input since calcium carbonate solubility decreases with rising temperature.

alkalinity.name: Total Alkalinity
alkalinity.shortDescription: The capacity of water to resist pH changes — a pH buffer.
alkalinity.longDescription: Total alkalinity (TA) measures the concentration of alkaline compounds — primarily bicarbonates, carbonates, and hydroxides — dissolved in pool water. It acts as a pH buffer, resisting pH swings caused by additions of acid, base, or CO₂. Low TA causes pH to swing wildly with minor chemical additions (pH bounce). High TA makes pH very difficult to lower and increases scaling tendency. Total alkalinity must be adjusted before pH — it determines how much chemical is needed for a given pH change.

lsi.name: Langelier Saturation Index
lsi.shortDescription: A composite score indicating whether water is balanced, corrosive, or scale-forming.
lsi.longDescription: The Langelier Saturation Index (LSI) is a mathematical model that combines pH, temperature, calcium hardness, total alkalinity, and TDS into a single balance score. A score of 0 means water is perfectly balanced for calcium carbonate. Negative values (below −0.3) indicate corrosive water. Positive values (above +0.5) indicate scale-forming water. The LSI is the final quality check in the water balancing process — if all individual parameters are in range but the LSI is out of range, the combination still needs adjustment.

gallons.name: Gallons
gallons.shortDescription: US liquid gallon — the standard unit of pool volume measurement.
gallons.longDescription: The US gallon (approximately 3.785 liters) is the standard unit for measuring pool volume in North America. All chemical dose calculations for pools require an accurate volume in gallons. Volume is calculated using length × width × average depth × 7.48 (gallons per cubic foot) for rectangular pools, with shape correction factors for other pool shapes. A 10% error in pool volume produces a 10% error in every chemical dose calculated.

liters.name: Liters
liters.shortDescription: SI unit of volume — 1 US gallon equals approximately 3.785 liters.
liters.longDescription: The liter is the SI unit of volume used in metric countries for pool measurements. One US gallon equals approximately 3.785 liters. While calculators on this site use US gallons as the primary unit, all conversions to and from liters are supported. Chemical doses calculated in metric units (grams per liter, or mg/L for ppm equivalents) are consistent with the same chemistry but expressed in metric terms.

ppm.name: Parts Per Million
ppm.shortDescription: The standard unit for measuring chemical concentrations in pool water.
ppm.longDescription: Parts per million (ppm) is the standard unit of concentration for pool chemistry parameters including free chlorine, alkalinity, calcium hardness, cyanuric acid, and TDS. 1 ppm equals 1 milligram per liter (mg/L) in aqueous solution. Most pool test kits and digital testers report results in ppm. The relationship between ppm and actual chemical dose is direct: 1 ppm in a 10,000-gallon pool corresponds to 8.34 mg of the substance dissolved in the water.

flow-rate.name: Flow Rate
flow-rate.shortDescription: The volume of water the pump moves per minute — a key factor in turnover rate.
flow-rate.longDescription: Flow rate is measured in gallons per minute (GPM) and represents how much water the pump circulates through the filtration system. The required flow rate for adequate filtration is calculated from pool volume divided by the target turnover time. Pump flow rate in real systems is lower than the rated maximum because of pipe resistance, filter restriction, and other head pressure losses. Variable speed pumps can be programmed to run at different flow rates at different times of day, reducing energy consumption while maintaining adequate filtration.
flow-rate.idealRange: N/A (calculated from pool volume and target turnover)

turnover-time.name: Turnover Time
turnover-time.shortDescription: The time required for the pump to circulate the entire pool volume through the filter once.
turnover-time.longDescription: Turnover time is the number of hours required for the pump to move the full pool volume through the filtration system. It is calculated as pool volume divided by pump flow rate. PHTA recommends a maximum turnover time of 8 hours for residential pools (one complete turnover in 8 hours or less). Shorter turnover times indicate better filtration — most high-quality pools achieve 6-hour or less turnovers. Hot tub turnover is faster due to smaller volume; the target is typically 2–4 turnovers per day.

pump.name: Pool Pump
pump.shortDescription: The motor and impeller assembly that circulates water through the filtration and chemical treatment system.
pump.longDescription: The pool pump is the heart of the pool circulation system. It draws water from skimmers and main drains, forces it through the filter, heater, and chemical feeders, then returns it through jets. Pump sizing is based on the required GPM for the target turnover time. Single-speed pumps run at one fixed RPM; variable-speed pumps (VSP) can be programmed to run at different speeds, reducing energy consumption by up to 80% compared to single-speed models. VSPs are now required by energy codes in many jurisdictions.

sand-filter.name: Sand Filter
sand-filter.shortDescription: A filter using silica sand to trap particles down to 20–40 microns.
sand-filter.longDescription: Sand filters use a bed of specially graded silica sand (#20 grade) to capture suspended particles. Water flows down through the sand, which traps debris, algae, and fine particles. When the filter pressure increases 8–10 psi above the clean baseline, the filter needs backwashing — reversing the flow to flush trapped material to waste. Sand should be replaced every 5–7 years. Sand filters have the coarsest filtration (20–40 microns) of the three main filter types but are the lowest maintenance.

cartridge-filter.name: Cartridge Filter
cartridge-filter.shortDescription: A filter using pleated polyester cartridges to trap particles down to 10–15 microns without backwashing.
cartridge-filter.longDescription: Cartridge filters use pleated polyester fabric cartridges to filter pool water. They provide finer filtration than sand (10–15 microns) without requiring backwashing — only periodic cartridge removal, rinsing with a hose, and occasional overnight soaking in cartridge cleaning solution. Cartridges should be replaced every 12–18 months. They are well suited to areas with water restrictions because they do not require backwash water. Flow resistance is higher than sand filters of the same size, which may require a larger pump.

de-filter.name: DE Filter
de-filter.shortDescription: A diatomaceous earth filter offering the finest filtration (3–5 microns) of any pool filter type.
de-filter.longDescription: Diatomaceous earth (DE) filters use a fine powder made from fossilized diatoms (microscopic algae) as the filter media. The DE powder coats internal grids or fingers, providing the finest filtration of any pool filter type — down to 3–5 microns. This makes DE filters excellent for pools requiring crystal-clear water. Maintenance involves backwashing (which removes the used DE) followed by adding fresh DE through the skimmer. DE must be handled carefully as fine particles can be an inhalation hazard. Internal grids require annual cleaning and periodic inspection.

skimmer.name: Skimmer
skimmer.shortDescription: A wall-mounted intake that removes floating debris from the pool surface before it sinks.
skimmer.longDescription: Pool skimmers are built into the pool wall at the water line. They use a weir (floating flap) to create a surface current that draws floating leaves, insects, sunscreen, and debris into a basket before the debris sinks to the pool floor. Most residential pools have one to three skimmers depending on size. The skimmer basket should be checked and emptied regularly — a clogged basket restricts pump flow. Never add granular shock directly to the skimmer; it can damage equipment. Skimmers also contain a suction port used during pool vacuuming.

heater.name: Pool Heater
heater.shortDescription: A device that raises water temperature using gas, electric heat pump, or solar energy.
heater.longDescription: Pool heaters come in three main types: gas heaters (natural gas or propane), electric heat pumps, and solar systems. Gas heaters heat water rapidly but have higher operating costs. Heat pumps are more energy-efficient in warm climates but heat slowly. Solar systems have no operating cost but depend on sun availability and add time to the system. All heater types affect pool chemistry: higher water temperatures increase chlorine demand, pH rise, and LSI scaling tendency. Heater bypasses allow chemistry adjustment at lower temperatures to extend equipment life.

salt-chlorinator.name: Salt Chlorinator
salt-chlorinator.shortDescription: An electrolytic cell that converts dissolved salt into hypochlorous acid to sanitize pool water.
salt-chlorinator.longDescription: A salt chlorinator (also called a saltwater generator or SWCG) uses electrolysis to convert sodium chloride dissolved in pool water into hypochlorous acid — the same active disinfectant as manually added chlorine. The cell consists of titanium plates coated with a precious metal catalyst. The pool still uses chlorine — it is simply generated on-site from salt rather than added directly. Salt cells have a lifespan of 3–7 years depending on water chemistry and maintenance. The cell requires specific salt concentration (usually 2,700–3,400 ppm) and proper water chemistry to avoid premature calcium scaling of the plates.

automatic-chlorinator.name: Automatic Chlorinator
automatic-chlorinator.shortDescription: An inline or offline device that dispenses trichlor tablets continuously to maintain free chlorine.
automatic-chlorinator.longDescription: Automatic chlorinators (erosion feeders) hold trichlor tablets or granules and slowly dissolve them as water flows through. Inline models are installed in the return plumbing after the heater. Offline models are connected via bypass lines. They automate baseline chlorine maintenance between manual chemical additions. Because trichlor contains CYA (58% by weight), regular use of tablet feeders gradually accumulates CYA in the water. Feeders should be set to maintain 1–3 ppm FC and supplemented with liquid chlorine or shock as needed.

chemical-feeder.name: Chemical Feeder
chemical-feeder.shortDescription: A device that automatically dispenses pool chemicals at a controlled rate.
chemical-feeder.longDescription: Chemical feeders include erosion feeders (for solid products), peristaltic pump systems (for liquid chemicals), and ORP/pH automated controllers. Automated chemical feed systems monitor ORP and pH in real time and inject the appropriate chemicals to maintain setpoints. These are common in commercial pool operations and increasingly available for residential pools. They reduce manual chemical handling and maintain more consistent water chemistry than periodic manual addition.

cover.name: Pool Cover
cover.shortDescription: A cover that reduces evaporation, heat loss, debris entry, and UV degradation of chemicals.
cover.longDescription: Pool covers serve multiple functions: safety (hard covers and nets prevent accidental entry), heat retention (solar and thermal covers reduce heat loss and heating costs), water conservation (reduce evaporation by up to 95%), chemical conservation (reduce UV degradation of chlorine and reduce debris-driven chemical demand), and debris exclusion (keep leaves and insects out). Hot tub covers are essential for heat retention and chemical stability. Safety covers are required by law in many jurisdictions for unattended residential pools. Solar covers (bubble covers) are the most common residential pool cover and offer excellent ROI through reduced heating and water costs.

shock-treatment.name: Shock Treatment
shock-treatment.shortDescription: Adding a large dose of chlorine or non-chlorine oxidizer to destroy combined chlorine, algae, and contaminants.
shock-treatment.longDescription: Shock treatment (superchlorination) involves raising free chlorine to a high level — typically 10 ppm for maintenance, 10× the combined chlorine level for breakpoint chlorination, or 30 ppm for algae recovery — to eliminate combined chlorine, algae, bacteria, and other contaminants. Use calcium hypochlorite (65%) or liquid chlorine (sodium hypochlorite) for chlorine shocking. Non-chlorine shock (potassium monopersulfate) oxidizes contaminants without adding chlorine — useful when swimming must resume quickly. Always shock after dark to prevent UV degradation of the added chlorine.

breakpoint-chlorination.name: Breakpoint Chlorination
breakpoint-chlorination.shortDescription: Adding chlorine at 10× the combined chlorine level to destroy all chloramines.
breakpoint-chlorination.longDescription: Breakpoint chlorination is the process of adding enough chlorine to destroy all combined chlorine (chloramines) in pool water. The breakpoint dose is approximately 10 times the current combined chlorine level. Below this threshold, adding chlorine merely adds to combined chlorine; above it, all combined chlorine is oxidized and destroyed. The term "breakpoint" describes the inflection point on the chlorine demand curve where adding more chlorine actually increases free chlorine rather than increasing combined chlorine. Combined chlorine above 0.5 ppm is the trigger for breakpoint chlorination.

backwashing.name: Backwashing
backwashing.shortDescription: Reversing water flow through a sand or DE filter to flush trapped debris to waste.
backwashing.longDescription: Backwashing is the process of reversing water flow through a sand or DE filter to dislodge and flush accumulated debris. It is initiated when the filter pressure gauge reads 8–10 psi above the clean baseline. The multiport valve is turned to "Backwash," the pump is run until water runs clear (typically 2–5 minutes), then switched to "Rinse" for 30–60 seconds to reseat the sand before returning to "Filter." Backwashing removes water from the pool — factor this into water level management. DE filters require adding fresh DE powder after backwashing to recharged the filter grids.

winterization.name: Winterization
winterization.shortDescription: The process of closing a pool or hot tub for the winter to prevent freeze damage.
winterization.longDescription: Winterization (pool closing) involves a specific sequence of steps to protect pool equipment and surfaces from freeze damage during cold weather: balancing water chemistry, adding winter chemicals (algaecide, scale inhibitor), draining water below skimmers and jets, blowing out plumbing lines, plugging returns, removing and storing equipment, and covering the pool. Hot tub winterization involves either proper insulation and continuous low-level heating, or full draining. Improper winterization is one of the most common and expensive pool maintenance mistakes.

pool-opening.name: Pool Opening
pool-opening.shortDescription: The spring start-up process to prepare a pool for the swimming season.
pool-opening.longDescription: Pool opening (spring start-up) is the systematic process of bringing a winterized pool back into service: removing the cover and cleaning it, removing winter plugs and reinstalling equipment, reconnecting the pump and filter, filling to proper water level, starting the pump and checking for leaks, then testing and balancing all water chemistry parameters before the first swim. Pool opening chemistry typically requires more adjustment than weekly maintenance because water chemistry changes significantly during winter shutdown. A complete water balance is the final step before opening for swimming.

water-replacement.name: Water Replacement
water-replacement.shortDescription: Partially or completely draining and refilling pool or spa water to reduce dissolved compound levels.
water-replacement.longDescription: Water replacement (partial or full drain and refill) is the only way to reduce CYA, calcium hardness, TDS, and salt when they exceed maximum levels. A partial drain replaces a percentage of the water — a 50% drain reduces all dissolved compounds by 50%. Hot tubs require complete water changes every 3–4 months due to high bather-to-water ratios that accelerate TDS and combined chlorine accumulation. Pool partial drains are typically 25–50% and are triggered by CYA above 80 ppm, calcium above 500 ppm, or TDS above 3,000 ppm.

filtration.name: Filtration
filtration.shortDescription: The continuous mechanical removal of suspended particles from pool water.
filtration.longDescription: Filtration is the continuous process of circulating pool water through a filter to remove suspended particles — algae, dust, debris, dead skin cells, and other particulate matter. Effective filtration requires adequate pump flow rate, properly sized filter, regular cleaning, and sufficient daily pump run time. Filtration does not replace chemical sanitization but works synergistically — the filter removes the physical matter that would otherwise increase chemical demand. The three main filter types (sand, cartridge, DE) differ in filtration fineness, maintenance frequency, and water usage.

testing.name: Water Testing
testing.shortDescription: Measuring pool water chemistry parameters using test strips, liquid kits, or digital testers.
testing.longDescription: Water testing is the foundation of pool maintenance. Accurate, regular testing of free chlorine, combined chlorine, pH, alkalinity, calcium hardness, and CYA enables correct chemical dosing. Test methods include: test strips (fast but less precise), DPD liquid test kits (more accurate, color-based), digital photometric testers (highest accuracy), and professional testing by a pool store. Testing frequency varies by parameter: FC and pH should be tested twice weekly; alkalinity and calcium monthly. Test before every soak in a hot tub.

sanitizing.name: Sanitizing
sanitizing.shortDescription: Maintaining an adequate residual disinfectant to destroy pathogens in pool water.
sanitizing.longDescription: Sanitizing is the ongoing process of maintaining sufficient disinfectant (free chlorine, bromine, or alternative) to kill bacteria, viruses, and other pathogens in pool water. Effective sanitization requires maintaining free chlorine above the minimum level for the current CYA concentration, ensuring pH is in the 7.2–7.6 range where HOCl is maximally effective, and providing adequate turnover for the disinfectant to contact all parts of the pool. Sanitizing is distinct from oxidizing — both are needed for safe, clear pool water.
sanitizing.idealRange: N/A (depends on disinfectant type and CYA)

oxidation.name: Oxidation
oxidation.shortDescription: The chemical destruction of organic compounds, combined chlorine, and contaminants in pool water.
oxidation.longDescription: Oxidation is the chemical reaction that destroys organic matter, combined chlorine (chloramines), swimmer waste, and other contaminants in pool water. While free chlorine both sanitizes (kills pathogens) and oxidizes (destroys organic matter), pools with high bather loads may have more oxidation demand than chlorine sanitization demand. Non-chlorine oxidizers (potassium monopersulfate, hydrogen peroxide) can handle the oxidation load while preserving free chlorine for sanitization. Regular oxidation keeps combined chlorine low, prevents chlorine odor, and maintains water clarity.

balancing.name: Water Balancing
balancing.shortDescription: The process of adjusting all chemistry parameters to achieve a stable, non-corrosive, non-scaling LSI.
balancing.longDescription: Water balancing is the comprehensive process of adjusting pH, total alkalinity, calcium hardness, CYA, and free chlorine to achieve a stable, safe, and non-damaging water chemistry. The correct order matters: adjust alkalinity first (it determines how much acid/base is needed for pH), then pH, then calcium hardness, then CYA, then chlorine. The final check is the LSI — if all individual parameters are in range, the LSI confirms the combination is balanced. Properly balanced water protects equipment, surfaces, and swimmers.

maintenance-checklist.name: Pool Maintenance Checklist
maintenance-checklist.shortDescription: A printable weekly pool maintenance checklist covering testing, cleaning, and chemical additions.
maintenance-checklist.longDescription: The Pool Maintenance Checklist is a free printable resource that guides residential pool owners through weekly pool care: testing water chemistry, adding chemicals, cleaning skimmer baskets, brushing walls, checking filter pressure, and verifying equipment operation. Following a consistent checklist prevents the buildup of problems that lead to expensive treatments.

maintenance-log.name: Hot Tub Maintenance Log
maintenance-log.shortDescription: A printable log for recording hot tub and spa water tests, chemical additions, and service notes.
maintenance-log.longDescription: The Hot Tub Maintenance Log tracks daily and weekly spa chemistry readings, chemical doses, filter cleaning, and water change dates. Consistent record-keeping helps identify patterns, troubleshoot problems faster, and demonstrate due diligence for vacation rental operators.

chemical-log.name: Pool Chemical Log Sheet
chemical-log.shortDescription: A printable log for tracking pool chemical inventory, purchases, and usage over time.
chemical-log.longDescription: The Pool Chemical Log Sheet provides a structured record of chemical purchases, storage inventory, and usage per maintenance session. It is especially useful for vacation rental operators who must demonstrate chemical compliance and for multi-property managers tracking chemical costs.

vacation-rental-checklist.name: Airbnb Pool Turnover Checklist
vacation-rental-checklist.shortDescription: A printable turnover checklist for vacation rental pool inspection and chemistry verification between guests.
vacation-rental-checklist.longDescription: The Vacation Rental Pool Turnover Checklist provides a structured protocol for testing, adjusting, and documenting pool chemistry at the start of each guest stay. It covers safety equipment inspection, water chemistry testing, chemical additions, filter check, and safety communication to incoming guests. Used consistently, it reduces liability exposure and ensures every guest has safe pool access.

water-test-sheet.name: Water Test Log
water-test-sheet.shortDescription: A printable log for recording water test results over time to track chemistry trends.
water-test-sheet.longDescription: The Water Test Log provides a structured format for recording all pool or hot tub chemistry test results over time: free chlorine, pH, alkalinity, calcium hardness, CYA, salt, and any notes on chemical additions or pool events. Tracking readings over time reveals chemistry trends, helps diagnose recurring problems, and supports informed decisions about when water replacement is needed.

opening-checklist.name: Pool Opening Checklist
opening-checklist.shortDescription: A printable step-by-step checklist for spring pool opening.
opening-checklist.longDescription: The Pool Opening Checklist guides pool owners through the spring startup process: removing the cover, reinstalling equipment, filling to proper level, starting the pump, and completing a full water balance before the first swim. It provides space for recording test results and chemical additions during the opening process.

closing-checklist.name: Pool Closing Checklist
closing-checklist.shortDescription: A printable step-by-step checklist for winterizing a pool.
closing-checklist.longDescription: The Pool Closing Checklist provides a structured process for winterizing a pool: balancing chemistry, adding winter chemicals, lowering water level, blowing out plumbing, installing freeze plugs, removing equipment, and covering the pool. Proper winterization prevents expensive freeze damage.

emergency-reference.name: Emergency Recovery Reference
emergency-reference.shortDescription: A printable quick-reference for emergency pool and spa recovery scenarios.
emergency-reference.longDescription: The Emergency Recovery Reference provides concise protocols for the most urgent pool chemistry situations: green pool recovery, zero chlorine restoration, chemical overdose response, and equipment failure response. Designed for vacation rental operators and property managers who need clear action steps for uncommon emergencies.

cloudy-water.name: Cloudy Water
cloudy-water.shortDescription: Water that lacks clarity due to suspended particles, chemical imbalance, or filtration issues.
cloudy-water.longDescription: Cloudy water can result from low free chlorine (allowing algae or bacteria to proliferate), pH or alkalinity out of range (causing precipitation or flocculation), calcium carbonate precipitation (scaling, especially after shock), high TDS, poor filtration (pump run time too low, dirty filter, inadequate turnover), or dissolved metals. The remedy depends on the cause. Start by testing all parameters, correcting chemistry, and running the filter continuously until clarity returns. Clarifier can help coagulate fine particles for the filter to capture.

green-water.name: Green Water
green-water.shortDescription: Pool water discolored green by algae bloom due to insufficient free chlorine.
green-water.longDescription: Green pool water is almost always caused by an algae bloom — typically green algae — resulting from insufficient free chlorine. Contributing factors include CYA too high (reducing chlorine effectiveness), missed shock treatments, heavy rain (diluting chlorine), extended periods without service, or pump failure. Treatment involves lowering pH to 7.2 to maximize chlorine activity, brushing all surfaces, shocking to 30 ppm FC, and running the filter 24 hours. The water may turn grey as algae dies, then clear over 24–72 hours as the dead algae is filtered out.

foaming.name: Foaming
foaming.shortDescription: Persistent foam on pool or spa water surface caused by surfactants, high TDS, or algaecide.
foaming.longDescription: Foam on pool or hot tub water is caused by surfactants — substances that lower water surface tension. Common sources include body oils, lotions, soap residue on swimwear, certain algaecides (polyquats), and high TDS. In hot tubs, foaming is more common due to smaller water volumes and higher bather loads. Mild foaming can be treated with an anti-foam agent as a temporary fix, but the underlying cause must be addressed: rinsing swimwear without soap, showering before entering, reducing algaecide dose, or changing the water if TDS is very high.

scaling.name: Scaling
scaling.shortDescription: White or grey mineral deposits on pool surfaces and equipment caused by over-saturated water.
scaling.longDescription: Scaling is the precipitation of calcium carbonate and other minerals onto pool surfaces, tile lines, plumbing, and equipment. It is caused by over-saturated water (positive LSI), which occurs when pH, calcium hardness, alkalinity, or temperature is too high. Scale deposits are hard and difficult to remove — prevention is far easier than remediation. Treatment requires lowering the LSI by adjusting pH, alkalinity, and calcium hardness. Existing scale can be removed with acid washing or mechanical removal, but this should be done by a professional to avoid surface damage.

corrosion.name: Corrosion
corrosion.shortDescription: Damage to pool surfaces and metal equipment caused by corrosive (low LSI) water.
corrosion.longDescription: Corrosion occurs when pool water is under-saturated with calcium carbonate (negative LSI), causing it to aggressively dissolve calcium from plaster, grout, and metal surfaces. Visible signs include pitting of plaster surfaces, etching of tile grout, staining from dissolved metals (green from copper, rust from iron), and corrosion of metal fittings. Contributing factors include low pH, low alkalinity, low calcium hardness, and high water temperature. Treatment involves raising the LSI by adjusting the relevant parameters. Ongoing corrosion from a heater indicates the LSI needs attention immediately.

algae.name: Algae
algae.shortDescription: Plant-like organisms that grow in pool water when free chlorine is insufficient.
algae.longDescription: Algae are plant-like microorganisms that grow in pool water when free chlorine drops below effective levels. Green algae is the most common and easiest to treat. Mustard (yellow) algae is more resistant and requires more aggressive treatment. Black algae develops deep root structures that penetrate pool surfaces, making it the most difficult to eradicate. Algae growth is fueled by nutrients (especially phosphates), warm water, sunlight, and insufficient chlorine. Prevention requires maintaining adequate free chlorine relative to CYA level at all times.

strong-chlorine-smell.name: Strong Chlorine Smell
strong-chlorine-smell.shortDescription: A pungent chlorine odor caused by chloramines, not excess chlorine.
strong-chlorine-smell.longDescription: The "strong chlorine smell" associated with pools is not caused by too much free chlorine — it is caused by combined chlorine (chloramines). When free chlorine reacts with nitrogen compounds from bathers (urea, ammonia, amino acids), it forms chloramines that have a strong, distinctive odor and are irritating to eyes and respiratory tract. Paradoxically, the solution is to add MORE chlorine (breakpoint chlorination) to destroy the chloramines, not less. A well-maintained pool with low combined chlorine should have little to no chlorine smell.

eye-irritation.name: Eye Irritation
eye-irritation.shortDescription: Swimmer eye irritation caused by chloramines or pH imbalance.
eye-irritation.longDescription: Eye irritation from pool water is most commonly caused by chloramines (combined chlorine) or pH outside the 7.2–7.8 range. Human tears have a pH of approximately 7.4 — water at the same pH is least irritating to eyes. At lower pH, the water is acidic and irritating; at higher pH, chlorine effectiveness drops and chloramines accumulate. The fix for chloramine-induced eye irritation is breakpoint chlorination. The fix for pH-related eye irritation is adjusting pH to 7.2–7.6.

skin-irritation.name: Skin Irritation
skin-irritation.shortDescription: Swimmer skin irritation caused by pH imbalance, chloramines, or high disinfectant levels.
skin-irritation.longDescription: Skin irritation after pool or hot tub use can result from pH too far outside the neutral range (below 7.0 or above 8.0), high combined chlorine (chloramines), very high free chlorine (above 5 ppm), high bromine (above 10 ppm), or individual sensitivity to pool chemicals. In hot tubs, the combination of warm water and concentrated chemicals increases sensitivity. Rinsing with fresh water immediately after exiting the pool significantly reduces chemical exposure. Persistent skin irritation despite normal chemistry may indicate individual chemical sensitivity.

low-chlorine.name: Low Chlorine
low-chlorine.shortDescription: Free chlorine below the minimum effective level for the current CYA concentration.
low-chlorine.longDescription: Low free chlorine is the single most common and dangerous pool chemistry problem. When FC drops below the minimum for the current CYA level, the pool loses its primary protection against pathogens and algae. Causes include: heavy bather loads, hot sunny weather (UV degradation), CYA too high (reducing chlorine activity), insufficient dosing frequency, or empty chlorinator. The remedy is immediate addition of chlorine to restore FC to the target range. If CYA is above 80 ppm, a partial drain may be needed before chlorine can be maintained effectively.

high-chlorine.name: High Chlorine
high-chlorine.shortDescription: Free chlorine above 5 ppm causing bleaching, eye/skin irritation, and swimmer discomfort.
high-chlorine.longDescription: High free chlorine (above 5 ppm) causes bleaching of swimwear, eye and skin irritation, and respiratory irritation in enclosed spaces. It occurs after an accidental over-dose, feeder malfunction, or over-shocking. The pool should be closed to swimmers until FC drops below 5 ppm (3 ppm for hot tubs). Natural dissipation by sunlight and time is the safest remedy. Sodium thiosulfate can neutralize chlorine in emergencies but should be used sparingly — reducing FC too quickly can cause a rebound. Running the pump without cover during daylight hours accelerates UV degradation of excess chlorine.

low-ph.name: Low pH
low-ph.shortDescription: Pool water pH below 7.2, causing corrosion, eye irritation, and equipment damage.
low-ph.longDescription: Low pH (below 7.2) makes pool water corrosive and irritating. Effects include: etching of plaster and grout surfaces, staining from dissolved metals, corrosion of metal equipment and fittings, eye and skin irritation, and degradation of seals and gaskets. Low pH is commonly caused by adding too much acid, CO₂ from bather respiration, heavy rain (which is naturally acidic), and naturally acidic fill water. Treatment involves adding soda ash (sodium carbonate) to raise pH, after first verifying alkalinity is in range.

high-ph.name: High pH
high-ph.shortDescription: Pool water pH above 7.8, reducing chlorine effectiveness and promoting scale formation.
high-ph.longDescription: High pH (above 7.8) significantly reduces free chlorine effectiveness — at pH 8.0, only 22% of FC is in the active HOCl form (compared to 67% at pH 7.2). High pH also promotes scaling (high positive LSI), causes eye irritation through a different mechanism than low pH, and can cause white cloudiness from calcium carbonate precipitation. High pH commonly results from adding too much soda ash, sodium bicarbonate increasing pH as a side effect, CO₂ off-gassing from aeration (waterfalls, jets), and some source water. Treatment involves adding muriatic acid (hydrochloric acid) or dry acid (sodium bisulfate).

swimming-pool.name: Swimming Pool
swimming-pool.shortDescription: A permanent or above-ground body of water designed for recreational swimming.
swimming-pool.longDescription: A swimming pool is any artificial basin filled with water for swimming, wading, or exercise. Pools range from small above-ground models to large in-ground installations. Standard pool chemistry applies to all pool types, with adjustments for surface material, volume, and usage pattern. Most residential pools hold 10,000–30,000 gallons and require weekly chemical maintenance.

saltwater-pool.name: Saltwater Pool
saltwater-pool.shortDescription: A pool that uses a salt chlorinator to generate chlorine on-site from dissolved sodium chloride.
saltwater-pool.longDescription: A saltwater pool is a chlorine pool that generates its own chlorine using a salt chlorinator (SWCG). The pool still contains and uses chlorine — the salt content (typically 3,000–3,200 ppm) is far lower than ocean water (35,000 ppm) and is often described as similar to natural tears. Salt pools still require the same chemistry balancing (pH, alkalinity, calcium, CYA) as traditionally chlorinated pools. Key differences include higher CYA requirements (60–80 ppm), consistent monitoring of the salt cell, and the risk of calcium scaling on the cell at low LSI.

indoor-pool.name: Indoor Pool
indoor-pool.shortDescription: A pool housed inside a building, requiring ventilation management and no CYA.
indoor-pool.longDescription: Indoor pools present unique challenges: without UV light, chlorine is not degraded and CYA is not needed (and is actually counterproductive in indoor settings). However, chloramines accumulate more noticeably because there is less air movement. Ventilation is critical — pool rooms must exchange air continuously to remove chloramine vapors and prevent moisture damage to the structure. pH tends to rise in indoor pools due to CO₂ off-gassing into enclosed air. Cyanuric acid should not be used in indoor pools.

outdoor-pool.name: Outdoor Pool
outdoor-pool.shortDescription: A pool exposed to direct sunlight and weather, requiring CYA stabilization of chlorine.
outdoor-pool.longDescription: Outdoor pools are exposed to UV light that rapidly degrades free chlorine. Cyanuric acid (CYA) is essential for stabilizing chlorine in outdoor pools — without it, sunlight can destroy the chlorine within 30–60 minutes. Outdoor pools also experience chemistry changes from rainfall, temperature variation, and seasonal sun intensity. Summer requires more frequent chlorine dosing due to both UV degradation and higher bather loads.

hot-tub.name: Hot Tub
hot-tub.shortDescription: A small, heated pool (75–500 gallons) used for relaxation and hydrotherapy.
hot-tub.longDescription: A hot tub (spa) is a small, heated body of water — typically 75–500 gallons — used for soaking, relaxation, and hydrotherapy. The chemistry challenges are significant: high water temperature accelerates chemical reactions and chlorine demand; small volume means even one bather produces a significant bather load relative to total water; the high bather-to-water ratio causes rapid chemistry changes. Hot tub water should be tested before every soak session and changed every 3–4 months under typical use.

swim-spa.name: Swim Spa
swim-spa.shortDescription: A larger spa (12–20 ft) with jets for swimming in place and hydrotherapy.
swim-spa.longDescription: A swim spa combines the exercise function of a lap pool with the hydrotherapy features of a hot tub. Typically 12–20 feet long and holding 1,000–2,000 gallons, swim spas have a jet system that creates a current for swimming in place. Chemistry management is similar to hot tubs but with a larger water volume, reducing the impact of bather load. Many swim spas have separate hot tub and swim sections with separate chemistry.

commercial-pool.name: Commercial Pool
commercial-pool.shortDescription: A public or semi-public pool subject to health department regulations and inspection.
commercial-pool.longDescription: Commercial pools (public pools, hotel pools, club pools) are subject to state and local health department regulations that typically require stricter chemistry standards than residential pools — often a maximum 6-hour or even 4-hour turnover rate, specific free chlorine and pH ranges, mandatory ORP monitoring, and documented chemical logs. Commercial operations also require trained operators and regular third-party inspections. The principles are identical to residential pool care but standards are higher and enforcement is regulatory.

vinyl-pool.name: Vinyl Pool
vinyl-pool.shortDescription: A pool with a vinyl liner surface requiring lower calcium hardness targets.
vinyl-pool.longDescription: Vinyl liner pools have a flexible PVC liner as the pool surface. They require lower calcium hardness (150–250 ppm) than plaster pools because the liner itself does not dissolve calcium. Low calcium is less of a concern for vinyl pools from a surface damage perspective, but very aggressive water can still attack metal parts and fittings. Vinyl liners can be bleached by direct contact with undissolved granular chemicals — always pre-dissolve shock and calcium chloride before adding. Liners typically last 8–15 years before replacement.

fiberglass-pool.name: Fiberglass Pool
fiberglass-pool.shortDescription: A pre-molded pool with a smooth fiberglass surface requiring moderate calcium levels.
fiberglass-pool.longDescription: Fiberglass pools have a smooth, non-porous fiberglass surface that is inherently resistant to algae (fewer attachment points) and requires less maintenance than plaster pools. Calcium hardness targets are lower (150–250 ppm) than plaster pools. Very low calcium in aggressive water can leach the gelcoat surface over time. The smooth surface also means less chemical demand overall. Fiberglass pools cannot be refinished in the same way as plaster, so maintaining proper water chemistry to protect the surface is especially important.

concrete-pool.name: Concrete Pool
concrete-pool.shortDescription: A plastered or pebbled concrete pool requiring higher calcium hardness (200–400 ppm).
concrete-pool.longDescription: Concrete pools (gunite or shotcrete) have a plaster, aggregate (pebble), or tile surface applied over a concrete shell. These surfaces are porous and contain calcium — aggressive water (low LSI) actively dissolves calcium from the surface, causing etching, pitting, and roughness. Calcium hardness must be maintained at 200–400 ppm for plaster pools to prevent surface damage. Concrete pools are durable and highly customizable but require more careful chemistry management than vinyl or fiberglass pools.

liquid-chlorine.name: Liquid Chlorine
liquid-chlorine.shortDescription: Sodium hypochlorite solution (10–12.5%) — the most commonly used liquid pool sanitizer.
liquid-chlorine.longDescription: Liquid chlorine is sodium hypochlorite (NaOCl) solution, typically sold at 10–12.5% available chlorine for pool use (compared to 5–8.25% for household bleach). It is the most widely used chlorine product for pool maintenance: fast-dissolving, no residue, does not raise calcium or CYA, and relatively inexpensive. Degradation: liquid chlorine loses approximately 20–30% potency within 60 days at room temperature and significantly faster in heat. Always buy fresh product and check the manufacture date.

calcium-hypochlorite.name: Calcium Hypochlorite
calcium-hypochlorite.shortDescription: Granular or tablet pool shock available at 65% or 73% available chlorine (cal-hypo).
calcium-hypochlorite.longDescription: Calcium hypochlorite (cal-hypo) is a dry granular or tablet chlorine compound available at 65% and 73% available chlorine — the most concentrated of common pool shock products. It raises free chlorine rapidly and is the preferred product for breakpoint chlorination and algae recovery. Unlike trichlor and dichlor, it does not add CYA. However, it does add calcium — relevant in pools with already high calcium hardness. Must be pre-dissolved in water before adding to the pool; direct application can bleach liners and damage surfaces.

sodium-dichlor.name: Dichlor
sodium-dichlor.shortDescription: A stabilized granular shock (56–62% available chlorine) that adds both chlorine and CYA.
sodium-dichlor.longDescription: Sodium dichloro-s-triazinetrione (dichlor) is a stabilized granular chlorine compound containing approximately 56–62% available chlorine and 57% CYA by weight. It dissolves quickly and is convenient for pool shocking, but each pound added raises CYA by approximately 6–7 ppm per 10,000 gallons. Regular use as a shock product will accumulate CYA rapidly. Best used sparingly when CYA needs to be raised simultaneously with chlorine at season opening or after a significant drain. Not recommended for routine shocking because of CYA accumulation.

trichlor-tablets.name: Trichlor Tablets
trichlor-tablets.shortDescription: Stabilized chlorine tablets (90% available chlorine) for use in automatic chlorinators and floaters.
trichlor-tablets.longDescription: Trichloro-s-triazinetrione (trichlor) tablets contain approximately 90% available chlorine and 58% CYA by weight. They dissolve slowly and are used in automatic chlorinators, floaters, and skimmer baskets for consistent baseline chlorination. Very acidic (pH ~2.9) — repeated use will lower pool pH and alkalinity over time. CYA accumulation from trichlor is the most common cause of high CYA in residential pools. Should not be mixed with calcium hypochlorite — fire and explosion risk.

muriatic-acid.name: Muriatic Acid
muriatic-acid.shortDescription: Hydrochloric acid (31.45%) used to lower pH and total alkalinity in pool water.
muriatic-acid.longDescription: Muriatic acid (hydrochloric acid, HCl) at 31.45% concentration is the standard product for lowering pH and total alkalinity in pools. It reacts quickly and is highly effective but requires careful handling — it is strongly corrosive and produces acidic vapors. Always add acid to water (not water to acid), pre-dilute in a bucket of pool water, and add near return jets with pump running. Dry acid (sodium bisulfate) is a safer-handling alternative that produces the same chemistry result. Store in original container away from chlorine products.

soda-ash.name: Soda Ash
soda-ash.shortDescription: Sodium carbonate — used to raise pH in pool water.
soda-ash.longDescription: Soda ash (sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃) is the standard product for raising pH in pool water. Unlike sodium bicarbonate, soda ash primarily raises pH with a modest effect on alkalinity. Pre-dissolve in a bucket of water before adding to prevent white cloudiness in the pool. Typical dose: 6 oz raises pH by 0.2 in a 10,000-gallon pool. Too much soda ash can cause temporary cloudiness from calcium carbonate precipitation.

baking-soda.name: Baking Soda
baking-soda.shortDescription: Sodium bicarbonate — the standard product for raising total alkalinity in pool water.
baking-soda.longDescription: Sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO₃), commonly called baking soda, is the standard product for raising total alkalinity in pool water. It raises TA with a modest, predictable pH increase (typically 0.1–0.2 pH units for a standard dose). 1.5 lbs per 10,000 gallons raises TA by approximately 10 ppm. Pre-dissolve in a bucket of pool water before broadcasting around the pool perimeter. Pool-grade sodium bicarbonate is identical in chemistry to food-grade baking soda but is sold in larger quantities.

calcium-chloride.name: Calcium Chloride
calcium-chloride.shortDescription: Used to raise calcium hardness in pool water.
calcium-chloride.longDescription: Calcium chloride (CaCl₂) is the chemical used to raise calcium hardness in pool water. It dissolves exothermically (generates heat) — always pre-dissolve in a large bucket of water before adding to the pool, or add very slowly near a return jet. Allow 4–6 hours for full distribution before retesting. 12 oz raises calcium hardness by approximately 10 ppm in a 10,000-gallon pool. Calcium hardness can only be lowered by partial drain and refill — there is no chemical that removes calcium from pool water.

stabilizer.name: Stabilizer / CYA Granules
stabilizer.shortDescription: Granular cyanuric acid product used to raise CYA to the target stabilizer level.
stabilizer.longDescription: Pool stabilizer (cyanuric acid granules) is added to outdoor pools at the start of the season to raise CYA to the target range (30–50 ppm for standard pools, 60–80 ppm for salt pools). It dissolves slowly — place in a nylon sock and hang in front of a return jet, or pre-dissolve in warm water. Allow 24–48 hours before retesting. Never add to an indoor pool or covered spa. Stabilizer is also added gradually by routine use of trichlor tablets.

pool-salt.name: Pool Salt
pool-salt.shortDescription: High-purity sodium chloride (99.8%+) for use in saltwater pool systems.
pool-salt.longDescription: Pool salt is 99.8%+ pure sodium chloride (NaCl) sold specifically for use in saltwater pool systems. It must be free of additives (no anti-caking agents, iodide, or ferrocyanide) that can stain pools and damage salt cells. Sold in 40-lb bags; a typical 20,000-gallon pool requires 350–400 lbs to reach the target 3,200 ppm from zero. Salt does not evaporate and only needs replacement after significant water loss.

cdc.name: CDC
cdc.shortDescription: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — a key authority on healthy swimming and recreational water illness.
cdc.longDescription: The CDC provides guidelines on healthy swimming, recreational water illness prevention, disinfection standards for public pools and water parks, and outbreak reporting. Their Model Aquatic Health Code (MAHC) provides science-based guidance used as the basis for many state pool health codes.

epa.name: EPA
epa.shortDescription: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency — regulates disinfectants including pool chemicals.
epa.longDescription: The EPA regulates the registration, labeling, and use of pesticides and disinfectants in the United States under FIFRA (Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act). Pool disinfectants — including chlorine products, bromine products, and algaecides — are regulated as pesticides by the EPA. EPA registration numbers on pool chemical labels confirm federal approval.

phta.name: PHTA
phta.shortDescription: Pool & Hot Tub Alliance — the primary industry trade association for pool and spa professionals.
phta.longDescription: The Pool & Hot Tub Alliance (formerly APSP) is the primary trade association for pool and spa manufacturers, builders, service technicians, and retailers. PHTA publishes the Pool & Spa Operator Handbook (the industry standard reference for pool chemistry) and the ANSI standards for pool design, construction, and safety. PHTA certifications (CPO, ATP) are the recognized professional credentials in the pool industry.

nsf.name: NSF International
nsf.shortDescription: NSF International — certifies pool and spa equipment and chemicals to safety standards.
nsf.longDescription: NSF International develops public health standards and certifies products including pool equipment, water treatment products, and chemicals. NSF/ANSI 50 covers pool and spa equipment and chemicals. NSF certification marks on pool products indicate independent verification of performance and safety claims.

taylor-technologies.name: Taylor Technologies
taylor-technologies.shortDescription: Taylor Technologies — manufacturer of professional pool test kits and the standard reference for pool chemistry calculations.
taylor-technologies.longDescription: Taylor Technologies is the leading manufacturer of professional pool and spa water test kits (the Taylor K-2006 is the gold-standard residential test kit) and the publisher of the Pool/Spa Water Chemistry book, which is the definitive technical reference for pool chemistry calculations, LSI factors, and treatment formulas. Taylor LSI factor tables and formulas are used as the basis for LSI calculations throughout the industry.

lamotte.name: LaMotte
lamotte.shortDescription: LaMotte Company — manufacturer of professional water testing equipment for pool and spa use.
lamotte.longDescription: LaMotte Company manufactures professional-grade water testing equipment including DPD colorimetric test kits, digital photometers, and test strips for pool and spa use. LaMotte products are widely used by commercial pool operators and certified pool operators for their higher accuracy compared to consumer test strips.

unit-ppm.name: ppm
unit-ppm.shortDescription: Parts per million — the standard concentration unit for pool chemistry.
unit-ppm.longDescription: 1 ppm = 1 mg/L = 1 part chemical per 1,000,000 parts water. Used for free chlorine, combined chlorine, alkalinity, calcium hardness, CYA, TDS, salt, metals, and phosphates.

unit-mg-l.name: mg/L
unit-mg-l.shortDescription: Milligrams per liter — numerically identical to ppm in aqueous solutions.
unit-mg-l.longDescription: In dilute aqueous solutions (including pool water), mg/L and ppm are numerically equal: 1 mg/L = 1 ppm. mg/L is the SI unit preferred in scientific contexts, while ppm is the practical shorthand used in pool industry applications.

unit-gallons.name: US Gallons
unit-gallons.shortDescription: US liquid gallon — the primary volume unit for pool calculations in North America.
unit-gallons.longDescription: 1 US gallon = 3.785 liters = 0.1337 cubic feet. Pool volume in gallons is used in every chemical dose calculation. 7.48 gallons per cubic foot is the standard conversion used in pool volume formulas.

unit-liters.name: Metric Liters
unit-liters.shortDescription: SI unit of volume. 1 US gallon = 3.785 liters.
unit-liters.longDescription: 1 liter = 0.2642 US gallons = 1,000 milliliters. Used in metric countries for pool volume measurement. Chemical concentrations in mg/L are equivalent to ppm.

unit-fahrenheit.name: °F
unit-fahrenheit.shortDescription: Degrees Fahrenheit — the standard temperature unit for pool and spa temperature in North America.
unit-fahrenheit.longDescription: Fahrenheit is the US standard for temperature measurement. Pool temperature targets: 78–84°F (residential pools), 100–104°F maximum (hot tubs). LSI temperature factor tables use °F. Conversion: °C = (°F − 32) × 5/9.

unit-celsius.name: °C
unit-celsius.shortDescription: Degrees Celsius — the SI temperature unit used in metric countries.
unit-celsius.longDescription: Celsius is the SI standard for temperature. Pool targets: 25–29°C (residential), maximum 40°C (hot tubs). Conversion: °F = °C × 9/5 + 32.

unit-minutes.name: Minutes
unit-minutes.shortDescription: Unit of time — used for pump turnover calculation and wait times after chemical additions.
unit-minutes.longDescription: Minutes are used in pool chemistry for: turnover rate calculations (Volume in gallons / GPM = turnover time in minutes), wait times after chemical additions, and filtration cycle timing.

unit-hours.name: Hours
unit-hours.shortDescription: Unit of time — used for turnover rate and pump run time calculations.
unit-hours.longDescription: Hours are the standard unit for expressing pool turnover time, pump daily run time, and wait times for chemical balancing. PHTA recommends a maximum 8-hour turnover time for residential pools.

unit-days.name: Days
unit-days.shortDescription: Unit of time — used for maintenance scheduling and chemical activity timelines.
unit-days.longDescription: Days are used for maintenance scheduling (test twice per week, shock weekly), CYA dissolution time (24–48 days), water change intervals for hot tubs (every 90 days), and chemical activity timelines.

unit-weeks.name: Weeks
unit-weeks.shortDescription: Unit of time — used for maintenance scheduling (weekly testing, weekly shock).
unit-weeks.longDescription: Weeks are the standard interval for pool maintenance activities: weekly water testing, weekly shock treatment (optional), weekly brushing and vacuuming, and weekly filter checks.

unit-months.name: Months
unit-months.shortDescription: Unit of time — used for seasonal maintenance intervals and hot tub water change schedules.
unit-months.longDescription: Monthly intervals are used for: calcium hardness and CYA testing (monthly), hot tub water changes (every 3–4 months), filter inspection, and salt level verification.
